claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing materials are predominantly governed by grain-boundary sliding.
Dynamic recovery modulates grain-boundary sliding through a balance between vacancy-diffusion-assisted dislocation climb and irradiation-induced defect-cluster pinning at grain boundaries.
Simulated fusion neutron irradiation at temperatures above approximately 1000 °C generates irradiation-induced defects in polycrystalline refractory metals or similar alloys.
Moderate irradiation doses can produce significant defects while remaining within dynamic-recovery limits.
Grain-boundary effects are pronounced within an unspecified grain-size range.
Grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for dislocation motion and plasticity.
Grain boundaries act as sinks for vacancies.
Irradiation-induced defect clusters localize at grain boundaries and act as pinning points that modulate grain-boundary sliding.
At high temperatures, vacancy diffusion enables dislocation climb and thereby facilitates dynamic recovery.
The combined action of dislocation climb and grain-boundary defect clusters increases plastic strain without reducing toughness by balancing mobility with localized strengthening.
High-temperature irradiated specimens will exhibit greater plastic strain than otherwise identical high-temperature non-irradiated specimens.
High-temperature irradiated specimens will maintain or improve toughness relative to otherwise identical high-temperature non-irradiated specimens.
Irradiated specimens will have a higher frequency of defect clusters at grain boundaries, correlated with enhanced grain-boundary sliding.
High-temperature annealing without irradiation permits dynamic recovery but lacks modulation by irradiation-induced defect clusters.
The unirradiated baseline will have lower plastic strain and toughness than the irradiated condition.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to polycrystalline refractory metals or similar materials at fusion-relevant temperatures, moderate irradiation doses, and an unspecified grain-size range.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to amorphous materials or under extreme irradiation where defect accumulation overwhelms dynamic recovery.
A controlled comparison can isolate irradiation by testing identical specimens at the same high temperature with and without simulated neutron flux.

Failure to observe a statistically significant plastic-strain increase with maintained or enhanced toughness, or failure to observe the predicted boundary-cluster/sliding relationship, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Defect clusters are characterized as grain-boundary pinning points, yet greater cluster frequency is predicted to enhance grain-boundary sliding. The hypothesis does not supply an intermediate mechanism explaining how increased pinning produces increased sliding, creating a directional tension in the proposed causal chain.
